title: Linear equations and formula rearrangement
objective: Isolate a specified variable, state any divisor restrictions, and verify a proposed solution by substitution.
why: A sensor gives you a voltage, but you need a temperature. A motion model contains time, but time is the quantity you do not know. Rearranging equations lets you use a relationship in either direction. The essential skill is preserving exactly which values satisfy it.

sections.heading: An equation makes a claim
paragraphs: An expression such as $3x+2$ represents a value once x is chosen. An equation such as $3x+2=11$ claims that two expressions have equal values. A solution is an input that makes that claim true. Here $x=3$ works because $3(3)+2=11$; $x=4$ does not because $14\ne11$.

To solve an equation, build a simpler equation with the same solution set. Such equations are equivalent. You are not moving symbols by a special rule: you are applying an operation to both sides and simplifying. This viewpoint becomes especially useful when the unknown is a formula parameter instead of x.

Numbers and units play different roles. If $V=IR$, then V is the numerical voltage in a stated unit, I is current, and R is resistance. The algebra works on the entire relationship. Later, checking units helps you catch a reversed fraction.

sections.heading: Operations that preserve the solution set
paragraphs: Adding or subtracting the same expression on both sides preserves equality when that expression is defined. From $3x+2=11$, subtract 2 from both sides: $3x=9$. Divide both sides by 3: $x=3$. Substitution into the original equation verifies the result.

Multiplying or dividing both sides by a known nonzero number preserves equivalence. Zero needs special care. Multiplying an equation by zero erases information: both sides become zero even when the original equation was false. Dividing by zero is undefined.

If the divisor contains an unknown parameter, state the nonzero condition before dividing. From $ax=b$, the expression $x=b/a$ applies only when $a\ne0$. If $a=0$, inspect the original equation $0=b$. If b is zero, every real x works; otherwise no real x works.

A reliable workflow is: expand carefully, combine like terms on each side, collect variable terms, collect constants, divide by a nonzero coefficient, and check the answer in the original equation. More than one order of valid steps can work. Choose an order you can explain.

sections.heading: Signs, fractions, and distribution
paragraphs: Parentheses describe a whole quantity. In $-2(x-3)$ the factor -2 multiplies both terms, giving $-2x+6$. A common error is writing $-2x-6$ because only the first sign was considered. Expanding back or checking a simple input can expose the error.

A fraction bar also groups its numerator. In $(x+1)/3=5$, multiply both sides by 3 to obtain $x+1=15$, then subtract 1. In $x+1/3=5$, only the 1 is divided by 3; this is a different equation. When typing, use parentheses to state which expression belongs in the numerator.

To clear several numeric denominators, multiply every term on both sides by a common multiple of those denominators. For $x/2+x/3=5$, multiplying by 6 gives $3x+2x=30$, hence $x=6$. Check: $6/2+6/3=3+2=5$.

Keep exact fractions until an approximation is requested. The value $1/3$ is not exactly 0.3333. In this lesson's exact-value fields you may type a fraction, a terminating decimal, or arithmetic such as $(7-2)/3$. An approximate decimal will not be treated as an exact recurring fraction.

sections.heading: One solution, every solution, or no solution
paragraphs: A linear equation can be written $ax+b=cx+d$. Subtract cx and b from both sides to obtain $(a-c)x=d-b$. If $a-c\ne0$, exactly one solution is $x=(d-b)/(a-c)$.

If the variable coefficients are equal, do not divide by $a-c$: it is zero. Compare the remaining constants instead. For $2(x+3)=2x+6$, expansion leaves $2x+6=2x+6$, so every real x is a solution. This is an identity.

For $2(x+3)=2x+7$, removing the equal variable terms leaves $6=7$. No choice of x can make that true. This is a contradiction and has no solution. A canceled variable does not automatically mean $x=0$.

A quick numerical example can disprove a claim, but a single successful input cannot establish an identity. To establish that every real input works in a linear equation, simplify both sides and show that the variable coefficients and constants agree.

sections.heading: Rearrange a formula, then interpret it
paragraphs: Consider $v=u+at$, a supplied model for final velocity from initial velocity, acceleration, and time. To isolate t, subtract u from both sides and divide by a: $t=(v-u)/a$, provided $a\ne0$. Substitution reverses the reasoning: $u+a((v-u)/a)=v$ under that condition.

If $a=0$, the original formula becomes $v=u$. If the given velocities agree, this model supplies no unique time; if they disagree, no time can satisfy the model. The zero-acceleration case is not solved by putting zero into the denominator.

For the supplied relation $V=IR$, isolating R gives $R=V/I$ when $I\ne0$. Algebraically, a negative nonzero I is allowed. Any requirement that a parameter be positive must come from the physical context and should be stated separately.

After rearranging, check units and plausible signs. A time computed from a velocity difference divided by an acceleration has units of time. A model may also require $t\ge0$. A mathematically valid solution outside the modeled interval should be reported as outside that model, rather than silently accepted as a physical answer.

examples.title: Variables on both sides

steps.reason: Distribute 3 to both terms inside the parentheses.
Combine the constants on the left.
Subtract 2x from both sides; the solution set stays the same.
Both original sides equal 25, which verifies the solution.

examples.conclusion: The only solution is $x=9$. The remaining coefficient of x was 1, so this was neither an identity nor a contradiction.

examples.title: Recover a temperature from a calibration formula
examples.prompt: A supplied linear model is $V=aT+b$. Solve for T, and then use $a=0.02$, $b=0.5$, and $V=1.7$. Assume V is in volts and T is in degrees Celsius over the calibrated range.

steps.reason: Subtract the offset b from both sides.
Divide both sides by the nonzero gain a.
Substitute the given readings. The gain has units of volts per degree Celsius, so the quotient has temperature units.
Substitute the temperature back into the original calibration formula.

examples.conclusion: The computed temperature is 60 degrees Celsius. If the gain a were zero, the voltage would not distinguish temperatures; the inverse formula would be unavailable.

guided.title: You finish the reasoning
guided.setup: Solve $4x-7=9$. The goal is to undo subtraction first, then undo multiplication.
before: Add 7 to both sides. The left side becomes 4x.
Fill in the right-hand value, then divide both sides by 4.

hints: The right side must receive the same addition as the left.
Compute 9+7, then divide that result by 4.
The right side is 16 and x is 4.
explanation: Dividing both sides by 4 gives $x=4$. Check: $4(4)-7=9$.

guided.after: If you needed a hint, that is useful practice. The independent checkpoint comes later with different numbers and no displayed solutions.

interaction.prompt: Transform $3x+6=18$ into $x=4$. Predict the effect of each operation before applying it. Try applying an operation to only one side and explain why it cannot be an equivalent step.

summary: Equivalent equations have the same solution set. Apply valid operations to both sides.
Distribute to every term and use parentheses to make fraction numerators clear.
A nonzero remaining variable coefficient gives one solution. A true constant statement gives all real solutions; a false one gives none.
State nonzero restrictions before dividing by a parameter, and inspect excluded cases in the original equation.
Verify by substitution, then check units and any contextual limits.
retrieval: Without reopening the examples, explain the three possibilities for ax=b. Then rearrange a different formula and state the divisor restriction.
